sonuc: Violation of Article 10 - Freedom of expression - {general} (Article 10-1 - Freedom of expression)
paragraflar: (Application no. 40838/23)
This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.
In the case of Taş v. Türkiye,
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:
Jovan Ilievski, President, Gediminas Sagatys, Hugh Mercer, judges, and Dorothee von Arnim, Deputy Section Registrar,

the application (no. 40838/23) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 9 November 2023 by a Turkish national, Mr Ersan Taş (“the applicant”), who was born in 1984, lives in Istanbul and was represented by Mr K. Altıparmak, a lawyer practising in Ankara;

the decision to give notice of complaint concerning Article 10 of the Convention to the Turkish Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Mr Abdullah Aydın, Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye, and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;
the parties’ observations;
the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the examination of the application by a Committee;
Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,
Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:
SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1. The application concerns a prison sentence combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, imposed on the applicant following his criminal conviction for the offences of insulting the President of the Republic and insulting a public official.

2. At the time of the events in question the applicant was the holder of an account on the social media platform then called Twitter. The applicant’s account, named “@06melihchina”, was followed by more than 55,000 users of the platform. It was a parody account that portrayed jokes concerning the then mayor of Ankara, İ.M.G.

3. On 24 September 2014 the official account of İ.M.G. on the same platform posted a photo and a mocking statement in respect of the then chairman of the main opposition party, K.K. On the same day, the applicant made a comment under that post. The applicant’s comment included a derisive image pertaining to the President and İ.M.G. accompanied by the following statement: “We continue to work and steal tirelessly with our President, God willing” (Cumhurbaşkanımızla birlikte hiç durmadan çalışmaya ve çalmaya devam ediyoruz Allah’ın izniyle).
4. On 17 December 2014 İ.M.G filed a criminal complaint against the applicant on account of the content of his comment.

5. On 26 September 2017 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance (hereinafter “the Criminal Court”) sentenced the applicant to eleven months and twenty days’ and ten months’ imprisonment for insulting the President of the Republic and insulting a public official on account of his functions, respectively. It decided, however, to suspend the pronouncement of the judgment under Article 231 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see, for the text of this provision at the material time, Durukan and Birol v. Türkiye, nos. 14879/20 and 13440/21, § 23, 3 October 2023) and to apply a five‑year supervision period.

6. On 9 November 2017 the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the objection lodged by the applicant against that decision, finding that it had been made in accordance with both procedural and substantial law.

7. On 20 December 2017 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, he complained, inter alia, about his conviction owing to the comment in question.

8. On 29 March 2023 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression, in a judgment grouping similar applications, in accordance with its findings in its Atilla Yazar and Others judgment (see, for detailed information regarding that judgment, Durukan and Birol, cited above, §§ 28-31).

9. To redress the violation, the Constitutional Court ordered a retrial and decided to send a copy of its judgment to the Criminal Court for the reopening of the criminal proceedings. Moreover, it ordered the reimbursement of the court fees paid by the applicant before the Criminal Court, as well as his legal representation costs. However, it rejected the applicant’s just satisfaction claims in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The decision was served on the applicant’s lawyer on 13 July 2023.
10. On 9 November 2023 the applicant introduced his application before the Court.
11. On the same day, the applicant lodged a petition with the Criminal Court seeking a retrial in order to secure the implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgment.

12. On 12 December 2023 the Criminal Court rejected the applicant’s request with a final decision, stating that the Constitutional Court had not yet delivered its decision concerning the applicant’s individual application.
13. On 15 November 2024 the Constitutional Court filed a petition with the Criminal Court requesting information on the retrial proceedings.
14. On 21 November 2024 the Criminal Court informed the Constitutional Court that the retrial proceedings had not been commenced, without providing any reasons.

15. In his application to the Court, relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complained that his right to freedom of expression had been breached on account of his conviction and prison sentence, combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, owing to a comment he had posted on social media.
alleged violation of article 10 of the convention
16. The Government raised several objections to the admissibility of the application.
Objection concerning victim status

17. The Government contended that the applicant did not have victim status as the Constitutional Court had acknowledged the breach of the applicant’s freedom of expression and afforded sufficient redress.

18. The applicant argued that the Constitutional Court’s judgment did not deprive him of his victim status. Firstly, the Constitutional Court had not awarded him any monetary compensation in respect of non‑pecuniary damage. Moreover, he had been unable to have the merits of his complaints examined by a domestic court for more than ten years. Furthermore, the Criminal Court had refused to reopen the criminal proceedings against him despite the Constitutional Court’s judgment. He had therefore been living under a continued threat of prosecution owing to his remarks in 2014, which had had a chilling effect on his freedom of expression.

19. A decision or measure favourable to the applicant is not, in principle, sufficient to deprive him of his status as a “victim” for the purposes of Article 34 of the Convention unless the national authorities have acknowledged, either expressly or in substance, and then afforded redress for the breach of the Convention (see Rooman v. Belgium [GC], no. 18052/11, § 129, 31 January 2019). An alleged loss of an applicant’s victim status involves, inter alia, an examination of the persistence of adverse consequences for the applicant after the decision (see Sakhnovskiy v. Russia [GC], no. 21272/03, § 67 in fine, 2 November 2010).

20. In this regard, the issue as to whether a person might still claim to be the victim of an alleged violation of the Convention essentially entails on the part of the Court an ex post facto examination of his or her situation (see Scordino v. Italy (no. 1) [GC], no. 36813/97, §§ 180-82, ECHR 2006-V).

21. In the present case, the Court observes that the Constitutional Court acknowledged the violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression. To redress the breach, it ordered the reopening of the judicial proceedings (see paragraphs 8-9 above). However, the Criminal Court refused to reopen the proceedings (see paragraphs 11-14 above), even though the Constitutional Court’s judgment ordering the retrial had already been delivered and sent to the Criminal Court (see paragraph 9 above).

22. The Court accordingly considers that the present case is distinguishable from previous cases in which it found that the applicants had lost their victim status as a result of the redress afforded to them through the reopening of the proceedings as indicated in the Constitutional Court’s judgments and the implementation of the Constitutional Court’s findings (see, for instance, Gündüz v. Türkiye (dec.), no. 3473/19, §§ 46-59, 29 April 2025, or Wikimedia Foundation, Inc. v. Turkey (dec.), no. 25479/19, §§ 34-51, 24 March 2022).

23. Having regard to this conclusion, the Court sees no need to further examine the applicant’s contention that he retained his victim status in the absence of an award of compensation by the Constitutional Court in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

24. In the light of the above and in the particular circumstances of the present case, the Court concludes that the domestic authorities failed to provide sufficient redress in respect of the breach of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression, which had been acknowledged by a Constitutional Court judgment. The Government’s objection regarding the applicant’s victim status must accordingly be dismissed.
Objection based on incompatibility ratione materiae

25. The Government alleged that the expressions used by the applicant had run counter to Article 17 of the Convention. They argued that the applicant’s complaints were incompatible ratione materiae with the provisions of the Convention on the grounds that the images and the statements he had used had constituted an attack on the honour and dignity of others.

26. The Court notes that it has already examined and dismissed a similar objection and, having regard to the content of the comments posted by the applicant (see paragraph 3 above), sees no reason to reach a different conclusion in the present case (see Durukan and Birol v. Türkiye, nos. 14879/20 and 13440/21, §§ 46‑47, 3 October 2023). Accordingly, this objection must also be dismissed.
Objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies

27. The Government invited the Court to dismiss the application as inadmissible for failure to comply with the requirement of exhaustion of domestic remedies on the grounds that the applicant had failed to lodge a fresh individual application with the Constitutional Court following the Criminal Court’s refusal to reopen the proceedings. They argued that the Constitutional Court was empowered to examine complaints concerning the non-implementation of its judgments.

28. The applicant contested the Government’s objection, arguing that he had already lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court in respect of his complaints. Requiring him to lodge a further individual application with that court following the non‑implementation of its judgment would risk creating an endless cycle. Moreover, he argued that the initial criminal proceedings had commenced more than ten years earlier, and that obliging him to lodge a second individual application would result in further significant delays.

29. The Court reiterates that the rule on exhaustion of domestic remedies is neither absolute nor capable of being applied automatically; in reviewing whether it has been observed it is essential to have regard to the particular circumstances of each individual case (see Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland [GC], no. 21881/20, §§ 138-43, 27 November 2023).

30. The principle of subsidiarity imposes a shared responsibility between the States Parties and the Court (see Grzęda v. Poland [GC], no. 43572/18, § 324, 15 March 2022). It presupposes that the domestic courts ensure rapid, adequate and effective protection of the rights guaranteed by the Convention. The credibility of the domestic remedies available thus depends not only on the legal context, but also on the tangible implementation of the decisions issued at the national level (see Kavala v. Türkiye (no. 2) [GC], no. 2170/24, § 116, 25 August 2026).

31. In the present case, the violation of the applicant’s rights was acknowledged by the Constitutional Court, which ordered the reopening of the proceedings to provide an appropriate redress to the applicant (see paragraphs 8-9 above).
32. However, the Constitutional Court’s judgment was given no practical effect in the domestic legal order on account of the decisions taken by the relevant first-instance court.

33. In the Turkish legal system, the Constitutional Court forms an integral part of the judiciary within the constitutional structure of Türkiye (see Şahin Alpay v. Turkey, no. 16538/17, § 117, 20 March 2018). Pursuant to Article 153 § 6 of the Constitution, the decisions of the Constitutional Court are binding on all State bodies and authorities (see Uzun v. Turkey (dec.), no. 10755/13, § 66, 30 April 2013, and Şahin Alpay, cited above, § 111). Moreover, pursuant to section 50 of Law no. 6216 on the establishment and rules of procedure of the Constitutional Court, where the Constitutional Court finds a violation on account of a judicial decision, it sends the file to the relevant court for the reopening of the proceedings and the latter shall deliver a decision with a view to putting an end to the violation found by the Constitutional Court (see, Şahin Alpay, cited above, § 52).

34. In the present case, the Court notes that the binding judgment of the Constitutional Court was not implemented by the first-instance court. The Criminal Court repeatedly refused to reopen the proceedings, despite the unsuccessful attempt made by the applicant and the communication by the Constitutional Court of its judgment through its internal correspondence (see paragraphs 9 and 11-14 above).

35. In the light of the particular circumstances of the present case, the Court finds it questionable whether the implementation of a second Constitutional Court judgment ordering the reopening of the proceedings following a fresh individual application, as suggested by the Government, would be ensured.

36. Furthermore, such a requirement would place an additional burden on the applicant while he had already made use of all ordinary domestic remedies in respect of the complaint he raised before the Court (see, mutadis mutandis, Micallef v. Malta [GC], no. 17056/06, §§ 57-58, 15 October 2009). Imposing such an obligation on the applicant would have required him to initiate yet another set of individual application proceedings at a stage where the Constitutional Court had already found a violation of his freedom of expression more than eight years after the commencement of the initial proceedings (see, mutatis mutandis, Bellizzi v. Malta, no. 46575/09, §§ 38‑45, 21 June 2011, and Saliba and Others v. Malta, no. 20287/10, §§ 74-80, 22 November 2011) despite the ongoing chilling effect of those proceedings that he complained about (see paragraph 18 above).

37. Moreover, in the Court’s view, such an obligation could risk the applicant being caught in a vicious circle where the failure of one remedy would constantly give rise to an obligation to make use of another one (see, mutatis mutandis, Gaglione and Others v. Italy, nos. 45867/07 and 69 others, § 22, 21 December 2010).
38. It follows that, in view of the specific circumstances of the present case, the Court rejects the Government’s objection based on the non‑exhaustion of domestic remedies.
Objection based on the allegedly manifestly ill-founded nature of the application

39. The Government argued that the complaints had been duly examined by the domestic courts. They contended, in particular, that the Constitutional Court had assessed the applicant’s complaints and found a violation of his freedom of expression. They accordingly urged the Court to declare the application inadmissible, asserting that it was manifestly ill‑founded.

40. The Court considers that the arguments put forward by the Government raise issues which require an examination of the merits of the complaint under Article 10 of the Convention, rather than an examination of its admissibility (Durukan and Birol, cited above, § 45).
41. The Court concludes that the application is neither manifestly ill‑founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. It must therefore be declared admissible.

42. The Government contended that the facts of the present case differed from those in Durukan and Birol (cited above) in the sense that the Constitutional Court had already found an infringement of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression in the light of its Atilla Yazar and Others judgment (see paragraph 8 above).

43. The Court considers that the criminal conviction of the applicant because of an image posted and a statement made on social media, and the imposition of a prison sentence combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment interfered with the applicant’s right to freedom of expression (compare also Durukan and Birol, cited above, §§ 55‑56 with further references). It further notes that it has already held in Durukan and Birol (cited above, §§ 66-67) that, as the Constitutional Court had concluded in its above-mentioned Atilla Yazar and Others judgment, Article 231 of the Code of Criminal Procedure – which provides for the suspension of the pronouncement of judgments – did not offer the required protection against arbitrary breaches by the public authorities of the rights guaranteed by the Convention.

44. In the present case, the Court has not found any fact or argument capable of persuading it to reach a different conclusion. The interference in question was thus not “prescribed by law” as required by Article 10 § 2.
45. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 10 of the Convention.
APPLICATION OF ARTICLE 41 OF THE CONVENTION

46. The applicant claimed a total of 12,700 euros (EUR) without separately specifying the amounts requested in respect of pecuniary and non‑pecuniary damage, as well as for the costs and expenses incurred before the domestic courts and the Court. He submitted the fee agreement concluded between him and his lawyer, and another document indicating that his lawyer had worked on the application for 47 hours, resulting in fees in the amount of EUR 4,700.
47. The Court does not discern any causal link between the violation found and the pecuniary damage alleged. It therefore rejects the claim under this head.

48. In respect of non-pecuniary damage, having regard to the circumstances of the case, the Court awards the applicant EUR 2,000, plus any tax that may be chargeable (compare also Durukan and Birol, cited above, § 73).

49. In respect of costs and expenses, having regard to the documents in its possession, the Court considers it reasonseable to award the applicant EUR 1,000, plus any tax that may be chargeable to him, and dismisses the remainder of the claim.
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT, UNANIMOUSLY,
Declares the application admissible;
Holds that there has been a violation of Article 10 of the Convention;

that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months, the following amounts, to be converted into the currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement:
EUR 2,000 (two thousand euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non-pecuniary damage; and
EUR 1,000 (one thousand euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable to the applicant, in respect of costs and expenses;

that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amounts at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points;
Dismisses the remainder of the applicant’s claim for just satisfaction.
Done in English, and notified in writing on 3 November 2026, pursuant to Rule 77 §§ 2 and 3 of the Rules of Court.
Dorothee von Arnim Jovan Ilievski Deputy Registrar President
